content: Childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) is a rare speech disorder that affects a child's ability to produce sounds, syllables, words, and sentences with precision, consistency, and appropriate rhythm. It is estimated to affect approximately 0.1% of the general population. The condition is characterized by three core diagnostic features: (1) inconsistent errors in the production of both consonants and vowels across repeated attempts at producing syllables or words, (2) prolonged and disrupted transitions between sounds and syllables, and (3) inappropriate prosody, which refers to the rhythm, stress, and intonation of speech. These features are widely accepted as diagnostic criteria for CAS, as outlined by the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) in 2007. The underlying cause of CAS is thought to be a deficit in motor programming or planning. This means that while children with CAS know what they want to say, they experience a breakdown in the ability to plan and execute the fine, rapid motor movements required for accurate speech production. In addition to speech difficulties, children with CAS may also exhibit impairments in other areas, such as non-speech oral motor function, dysarthria (a motor speech disorder), language development, phonological production, phonemic awareness, metalinguistic skills, and literacy. These impairments may occur individually or in combination. Currently, there is a lack of high-quality evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to guide the treatment of CAS. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of speech and language interventions for children and adolescents with CAS, as delivered by speech and language pathologists or therapists. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as well as trial registries, up to April 2017. Reference lists of included studies were reviewed, and additional information was sought from authors of published studies, experts, and professional groups in the fields of speech and language therapy and linguistics. The review included RCTs and quasi-RCTs involving children aged 3 to 16 years who were diagnosed with CAS by a speech and language pathologist or therapist. Studies were grouped based on the type of treatment provided. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias and the quality of evidence using the GRADE framework. Only one RCT met the inclusion criteria for this review. This study, conducted in Australia, was funded by several organizations, including the Australian Research Council and the University of Sydney. It involved 26 children aged 4 to 12 years with mild to moderate CAS of unknown cause. The study compared two interventions: the Nuffield Dyspraxia Programme-3 (NDP-3) and the Rapid Syllable Transitions Treatment (ReST). Participants were randomly assigned to one of the two treatments, which were delivered intensively in one-hour sessions, four days a week, for three weeks. The therapy sessions were conducted in English by speech pathology students at a university clinic. Outcomes were assessed at multiple time points: before therapy, immediately after therapy, one month post-therapy, and four months post-therapy. However, this review focused on outcomes at one month post-therapy. By the four-month follow-up, many participants had resumed their usual treatment with their speech and language pathologist, introducing potential bias. As a result, the four-month outcomes were excluded from further analysis. The study found that both NDP-3 and ReST led to improvements in speech outcomes at one month post-therapy. For three specific outcomes, NDP-3 showed slightly greater improvements than ReST: (1) accuracy of production on treated words, (2) speech production consistency (measured using the inconsistency subtest of the Diagnostic Evaluation of Articulation and Phonology [DEAP] test), and (3) accuracy of connected speech (assessed by imitated word accuracy in connected speech involving at least three-word combinations). However, the differences between the two treatments were minimal. For accuracy of production on non-treated words, ReST demonstrated a marginally greater effect than NDP-3. The study did not assess functional communication as an outcome. The quality of evidence was downgraded to moderate due to imprecision, as only one RCT was included in the review. No formal statistical comparisons were conducted by the original study authors to determine whether one treatment was superior to the other. Therefore, it is not possible to reliably recommend one treatment over the other. Additionally, there is no evidence to determine whether either treatment is more effective than no treatment or standard treatment. In conclusion, there is limited evidence to suggest that both NDP-3 and ReST, when delivered intensively, may improve word accuracy, speech production consistency, and connected speech accuracy in children aged 4 to 12 years with CAS. However, the study did not evaluate functional communication, and further research is needed. Additional RCTs replicating this study would strengthen the evidence base. Furthermore, future research should explore other interventions, different age groups, and populations with CAS, including those with co-occurring disorders.
